focus_profile.learning_goal: 关注 CSM、EV/NBV、资本补充、偿付能力、利润桥和管理层战略叙事。
tasks: 选一家公司，写出财报利润、CSM 和资本动作之间的关系。
记录一个资本补充或分红政策变化对业务增长的含义。
复习一个 IFRS 17 概念并写成自己的解释。

daily_concept.definition: 超过自留额后由再保险人承担约定层级损失的非比例再保险安排。
daily_concept.exercise: 画出 1-in-100 巨灾损失下，自留额、限额和恢复保费对净损失的影响。

items.rss_description: Independent Agents - A Forward View Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:36 Economic simulations now forecast fiscal health across 1,900 U.S. localities, helping agents anticipate consumer affordability shifts and community financial stress. October 23, 2026 Image Local agents swim in the waters around them, and while a rising tide lifts all boats, that sucking sound before a tsunami hits shore is a clear signal that locality risk is a constant. It's good to be lucky with a rising tide, but luck is not a strategy. Simulations of the world are a way to describe observed reality and anticipate change, and modeling the changing economic tides of every locality in America (call that a list with 1,900 locations) is a good way to both reflect on what has happened since COVID-19 and to help those agents see what's coming next. Modeling Communities Like We Model Weather We simulate weather daily to anticipate storm tracks and estimate damage. We simulate climate change with variation in sea level, flood plains, and riverbanks. We simulate fire spread, hail fall, straight-line wind… and so, too, we should simulate the local economies of 1,900 communities across America. In a consumer-driven economy, simulating how America spends is like watching a developing hurricane pattern off the shore – is it intensifying or waning, is it heading for land or staying off the coast, what amount of intrusion to interior geographies will a footprint create, and will there be additional risks set in motion as the dynamics unfold, including supply chain and demand patterns that may also be interrupted or surged? Affordability and Fiscal Health as Key Signals Just as a student loan may go unpaid if post-graduate incomes are low, the choices households and individuals make on debts to service and debts to default are mirrored at businesses, organizations, and local communities, cities, and municipalities. These local priorities of affordability affect decisions on risk transfer and affect premiums – agents sit amid it all. (See this article on a data source to predict financial health, going beyond the backward-looking credit reports that insurers use.) Affordability is a key signal, as is the fiscal health of a locality. When you combine these with the inflows and outflows of households and businesses, any agency can make a plan for the year or two ahead and set in motion a process for continually navigating their locales. Looking Backward: The Affordability Crisis People living in houses and driving cars work at businesses and spend money in their communities. Unsurprisingly, changes in the economies of those communities are both observable and predictable. That matters to local agents. Looking backward, hindsight is usually 20/20 – higher uninsured driver populations occurred where affordability was lowest. More UM/UIM claims drive insurance costs higher, and rates may go up even further. In an economic downswing, rising costs and flat to slow wage increases force more budget stress on consumers. Where job loss escalates stress, things twist up even faster. Not only do consumers decide not to be insured, but they also change other spending habits. More businesses fail when customers can no longer afford them. Collections of tax revenue suffer when high earners migrate away and when business activity slows or falters. Taxes suffer further when sales slump, and property values deteriorate. These can lead to cuts in community services, and spiral from there. Emerging Patterns: From Data Centers to Remote Work Independent agents, brokers of all sizes, carriers, wholesalers, specialty, excess, and MGA/MGUs all compete in these predictable localities. And predictions for consumers, businesses, and even the localities are proving their value in understanding and pricing risk. Some localities see changes that are from emerging patterns of life and risk, like hyperscale data centers. Other changes are more subtle, like a work-from-anywhere job landscape that allows high earners to live wherever they want. Or what happens when AI shifts work tasks in legacy workflows or creates new ways of working? Boomtowns to ghost towns and everything in between paint the map of America -- parcel-by-parcel, building-by-building, business-by-business, organization-by-organization, job-by-job, and so, too, insurance and risk management dynamics. Some things change very slowly, while others shift abruptly, but the profound effect of "work anywhere" from COVID may be the most significant overarching impact in our generation and the next. Anticipating Economic Consequences We anticipate sudden changes to life patterns in a variety of peril-driven scenarios – hurricane, tornado, fire, severe convective storm – as well as in environmental scenarios like sea level change, cyclical patterns like El Niño, and even major disruptions like power outages, transportation interruptions, and cyber interference. Anticipating economic consequences, especially shifts in contribution to cash flow in community capital assets and liabilities, is another risk in the underlying infrastructure where all the other risks interact. Thriving localities add services and amenities, which attract more growth. Dwindling localities lay off public workers and renegotiate long-term liabilities while trying to improve local revenues with more taxes and fees. Debt offerings and the ability to service debt obligations are then most comparable to Ernest Hemingway's famous line on personal bankruptcy – which happens "gradually, then suddenly." New Analytics for Local Planning Analytics now exist for consumers, businesses, and their communities across the 1,900 localities that make up the investable and insurable economies of America. This observability of a locality, its finances, its threats/opportunities, and its ability to service its debts and obligations is summed across the consumer and business mix of their constituents and forecast against those changing elements to portray current and future years' planning horizons. Local agents can take heed. Situations with imminent insolvency are expected to make certain choices, while growth-busting upside creates better problems. Adapting to Local Reality While agents can always relocate, they are more likely to need to adapt to their local reality. While premium forecasts and business mix are constantly used in distribution planning and customer appetite focus, the pace of change has accelerated inside of the existing process steps. Using a locality stress index along with existing forecasts and affordability measures will make agents smarter in their marketplaces and quicker to react to change. This means that in troubled areas, expect more business failures, lapses, and non-payment of premiums in a dwindling premium pattern, yet a rise in risk for fraud, theft, and malicious mischief, including a heavier threat of arson. This includes household stress, too, where skyrocketing base rates have pushed daily budgeting stress onto most households for car and homeowner insurance into an affordability squeeze where many drivers are underinsured, overcommitting to large deductibles, or going all the way to lapsing insurance entirely and becoming uninsured drivers. What does luck look like? A common quote from successful businesses – "It's better to be lucky, even if you're good." Never has that been more relevant than today, as changes in local luck have magnified in recent years. Some places have a deep downside – rising taxes, failing businesses, public service degradation, municipal financial stress, drops in quality of life generally, and the ensuing changes in household composition from thriving to just holding on. Some places have all sunshine -- growth in incomes, formation of new jobs, infrastructure improvements, and engaged public services. To live in an uninvestable locality is the hallmark of being unlucky. The endpoints are always locality-based. It is where people live, where businesses operate, and where municipal authorities administer. For an agent, the forward look in these markets is flat to down. Fewer businesses for fewer booming households means fewer insurable assets. Even if premiums rise and commissions float with them, the total insurance value opportunity won't be in a boom cycle. The larger concern is a doom cycle. Investors are aware of the general migration trend outlined in this recent Census article , whereby large metro areas are losing residents, while many smaller metro areas are growing. Details matter, and this is where data and analytics add critical value: High earners are migrating away from large metro areas in fiscally troubled states. They are migrating to small and mid-sized metro areas: Boise, Idaho; Frisco, Texas. High earners are responsible for the majority of personal and property taxes, new business formation, and capital investments. Scoring the 1,900 Localities Across the observed 1,900 cities, the municipalities, consumers, and businesses are scored based on their future fiscal viability and likelihood to default across a set of debts (everyday bills, credit cards, car loans, mortgages, business loans, pension commitments, municipal bonds, etc.). Ranked near the top of the list is St. George, Utah, with a short-term debt ratio of 0.31, which represents total liabilities divided by total assets. St. George is representative of 60 mostly mid-sized "under the radar" cities that have low legacy liabilities and sustainable budgets and are growing their populations with a healthy taxpayer base. This is where you can feel comfortable doing business for the long term. Lucky local agents! Then there are plenty of typical "middling" cities, with budgets that are not sustainable over the long term due to underfunded pension and benefits liabilities. Steady as she goes for the next few years. On the other side of the scale – consider a poster child for fiscal mismanagement to the extent it appears on a list titled Uninvestable Cities. These cities are laying off public sector workers today as they struggle with revenue shortfalls. Most of these cities meet the technical definition of insolvency. They appear to have accelerating financial deterioration over the next 24 months, resulting in a highly likely outright fiscal crisis. Envision trying to do business in a city where high earners (lowest risk, rational decision-makers) are leaving. The businesses are shuttering, as well. New business formation is almost non-existent. The city struggles to fund basic services, while raising taxes. The residual population has lower FICO scores. Crime, including costly fraud, rises. The Resilience of Independent Agents Every year another study predicts the demise of independent agents. They are getting too old; they can't scale to digital; they can't compete with changing technology… add in AI. Yet every year independent agents remain a dominant force in commercial insurance and have never failed to impress in personal lines. Watch how they adapt across 1,900 localities as a way to keep insuring America. ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS PARKING LOT What has changed is almost everything all at once. Blame it on remote work options, but look at how many high-earner households opt to relocate for better taxes, better weather, better schools, better anything. Blame it on migration, but the businesses and services they need will follow them, while the ones that used to serve them will feel the loss. Blame it on anything you like, but the undeniable facts are that no one relocates to a state; they move to a specific location. The imbalances from losing localities to gaining localities are seen in shifts in income, housing, business formations/failures, and municipal financial resilience. To assess health, a current approach ties to the capital markets where municipalities trade their debt. Using a locality lens, it is possible to observe the condition of consumers, businesses, and municipalities. With modern data and analytics, we can track changes over time. Did all three (consumer, business, municipality) improve, stay the same, or deteriorate in the last few years? What is the effect of these local changes, and how fast are changes now occurring? What is in store for the next couple of years? The US is in the early stages of an economic transformation, by locality, and that means insurance agents have both local threats and opportunities. Like Detroit filing Chapter 9 bankruptcy in 2013, it is conceivable that other major cities may follow suit. No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

items.title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.original_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_description: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer? AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:19 Blocking Meta's AI agent on your website won't stop it from calling. Insurers need a plan to handle these calls. October 22, 2026 Image A consumer's AI agent can now call an insurer and ask for a quote. The possibility of such calls leaves carriers with two bad options: putting a licensed person on the line with a machine, or risk hanging up on a real person. Both options are wrong. There's a third. The AI phone calls are already happening. Reuters reported that people using Meta's Muse, the personal AI agent launched in the U.S. this past September, can have it call businesses to book appointments, check inventory or get quotes from contractors. A Meta employee testing this feature said an insurer kept hanging up on Muse after realizing it was an AI caller. At InsureTech Connect in Las Vegas, Steve Rullo, who is Guardian Life's chief digital and technology officer, told Insurance Business , "We are already seeing providers calling in for verification of benefits with AI." He described healthcare providers using AI to verify patient benefits, often for an entire list of patients in a single call. The Debate Is About Websites Since Muse launched, carriers and marketplaces have been deciding whether to allow it access. Insurify quickly blocked Muse, saying it "risks stripping carrier quotes of critical contextual information." Co-CEO Giorgos Zacharia explained, "A quote without its context is not a fair comparison. It is a number." Shortly afterward, Kin announced that it would let Muse crawl its site so customers can shop for quotes , and Zebra announced an integration the following day. Employers, a workers' compensation insurer, told Dig-In it doesn't allow third-party AI agents like Muse to access its operational systems or customer data. Each of those decisions is about access to a website or system. None of them covers phone calls, and blocking Muse online won't stop it from calling. I expect insurers will get a lot more of these calls. Handled the old way, they're a cost. Handled well, every one is a quote in front of a real shopper. That's where the real opportunities are. The Talking Is About 5% of the Value The answer is simple: AI for AI, humans for humans. Let AI answer calls from other AI, and let people answer calls from people. This way, a family dealing with a flooded basement won't be stuck on hold while a licensed agent talks to a bot. Most voice AI answers the phone, then sends the caller through a phone menu or to a person. That's 5% of the value. The other 95% is the work behind the call: pulling up the policy, filing the claim, writing the result back to the core system. If AI can handle a machine caller's request at this level, no person needs to pick up, and licensed people can focus on judgment calls, like denied claims. Most carriers aren't there yet. According to KPMG International's report Unlocking AI value in insurance , only 29% of respondents use AI agents or automation for end-to-end processes. Rullo said Guardian will keep people involved in its AI processes: "We'll still have a human in the loop." For some risk profiles, he said, Guardian wants alerts on exceptions instead of reviews of every transaction. People should own the decisions. They shouldn't have to answer every call. You Can't Always Tell Who Is Calling Carriers also can't always tell if a caller is a machine or a person. Reuters reported that Meta tested having human contractors make some Muse calls without telling the other party. A Meta vice president said the test without proper disclosures "was a miss," and Reuters said Meta has rolled back that test for now. So a call that seems to come from an AI agent might actually be from a person. Zacharia told Dig-In that Muse got around Insurify's bot detection and didn't identify itself. A system designed to resolve requests can help both human and AI callers. A system that only routes calls can't. Policyholders Already Draw the Line In Liberate's September survey of 1,001 U.S. claimants, 50% said they would prefer a claim paid in 60 seconds with no human contact over talking to a person within 10 minutes and getting paid in three days. Another 41% preferred a person on the phone. Of those who chose the fast payout, 55% still want a human involved in every denial. Fast on yes. Human on no. Across the whole survey, 61% say a human must review every denial. In the same survey, 86% want to be told when AI touches their claim. A Hi Marley survey of 550 senior property and casualty decision-makers and 2,000 policyholders in the U.S. and Canada highlights the gap carriers need to close. Eighty-five percent of executives think AI will build customer trust, but only 40% of policyholders agree. Ninety percent of policyholders said it's very or extremely important to know when they're interacting with AI, and two-thirds said their biggest worry is not being able to reach a human when it matters. Three Rules for Carriers First, use insurance-specific AI that works within your core systems to answer calls from machines. Sending a bot to a phone menu or a person wastes time and doesn't solve the problem. Second, keep a licensed person on every denial, no matter what else the AI handles. Third, be transparent about AI on both sides. Let people know when they're talking to AI, and expect AI callers to do the same. If carriers follow these rules, they can answer every call, whether it's from a person or an AI. The shopper using a machine gets a response, and the family with a flooded basement gets to talk to a real person. Insurance has always wanted to answer everyone who calls. Now it can. Amrish Singh

items.title: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges
items.original_title: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges
items.rss_title: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges
items.rss_description: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges Claims ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:52 Hurricane Isaias shows how quickly claims surge after quiet periods, straining leaner teams to review complex restoration invoices thoroughly. October 29, 2026 Image Hurricane Isaias spun up in the Gulf of Mexico and made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm on Oct. 9, just two days after becoming the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, the latest first hurricane in more than a century. Its sudden arrival is a reminder of how quickly a quiet claims environment can change. For property claims teams, the workload extends well beyond the initial wave of reported losses. Damage to hotels, apartment communities, retail centers and industrial properties can lead to large restoration projects and complex invoices that arrive over the weeks and months that follow. Early modeled estimates of privately insured losses range from $1 billion to $2 billion (Verisk) to $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion (Moody's RMS). While AM Best expects it to be an earnings event for insurers rather than a capital event, the storm created a substantial uptick in work for claims and restoration teams. The aerial imagery firm Vexcel counted about 17,860 damaged structures across Florida, Alabama and Mississippi, including more than 3,100 with major damage. A high-rise condominium resort on Pensacola Beach lost windows across two towers, and an apartment complex in Milton, Fla., lost much of its roof. Damage like that becomes restoration projects, and restoration projects become invoices. Isaias follows a prolonged stretch of slower claims activity. Industry data puts commercial property claims at 710,000 in 2025, down from 910,000 in 2023. A separate measure, U.S. property claim assignments , fell 12% year over year in the second quarter of 2026 and ran 13% below the five-year average, extending a four-year decline. These are different Verisk datasets, but both point to a slower claims environment. More of the work that remains also arrives in bursts: catastrophe claims made up 43% of second-quarter volume, up from 34% five years earlier. No claims organization can staff indefinitely for a catastrophe-level workload during a stretch like this. Nor should it. Teams that have adjusted staffing and resources to match lower demand face a particular challenge: claims volume can rebound much faster than review capacity can be rebuilt. When restoration invoices pile up, those leaner teams face a difficult trade-off. Bills can wait for a thorough audit, extending claim cycle times, or move through with less scrutiny, increasing the risk of leakage. Automation offers a way to absorb more work without having to rebuild the entire manual review operation. The surge also has a long tail. When Hurricane Sally struck the same stretch of coast in 2020, Florida insurers had closed about two-thirds of residential claims six weeks later, but only 13% of commercial property claims. Hurricane Ian made landfall in Florida on Sept. 28, 2022. In the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation's March 4, 2025, snapshot , 96% of the 789,066 reported Ian claims were closed. Yet 6,628 of the 32,850 commercial property claims remained open nearly two and a half years after the storm. Those figures do not establish whether the delays involved coverage, reconstruction, invoice review, or disputes. They do show how long commercial claims work can continue after the initial surge. The bottleneck moves as the claim progresses An initial wave of assignments is only the beginning. Adjusters must address coverage, communicate with insureds, inspect damage, review scopes and estimates, and coordinate recovery. Restoration invoices arrive as work progresses, often while those adjusters are still managing both new and existing claims. Large restoration projects can involve multiple crews, weeks of drying equipment, substantial material charges, and several subcontractors. The resulting invoices can be complex even under normal conditions. When many arrive together, claims teams face two pressures at once: more invoices to review and more work required to review each one thoroughly. An invoice is not simply a total to approve. Time-and-materials bills can require checking labor hours and classifications, equipment usage and duration, agreed rates, materials, subcontractor charges, markups, and arithmetic. A reviewer may need to compare the invoice with supporting records and the work performed. That takes time, and the work does not become less necessary because the team has fewer people available. Both delayed reviews and unsupported payments carry consequences for the insured, the carrier, and the restoration contractor waiting to be paid. Adding more reviewers can help, but it takes time to find, train, and coordinate them. It also raises the cost of handling a temporary spike. The more useful question is which repeatable parts of review can be completed consistently without requiring a few more hours of specialist time for every additional invoice. How automation can absorb a surge AI-enhanced automation can help teams review restoration invoices faster by extracting and sorting line items and running calculations to identify charges that need a closer look. During a surge, these capabilities support consistent, thorough review. AI can help turn invoice documents into organized data, while programmed audit rules check calculations and compare charges with agreed rates or benchmarks. The adjuster or specialist still has to consider the work performed, evaluate the findings, and resolve disagreements. Automation reduces the manual checking that precedes those decisions. Rest-Assured has pioneered the use of AI-enhanced automation in restoration invoice auditing. Property insurers have used the platform to audit nearly $1 billion in property restoration invoices, uncovering documented findings to guide claims professionals through review and resolution. Measure the effect on the claim The right measure is not merely how fast an audit comes back. Claims leaders should look at the time from invoice receipt to a documented review, how long exceptions take to resolve, the rate of confirmed findings, the cost per review, and whether payment disagreements are cleared sooner. Those measures show whether faster processing is actually helping the claim move toward resolution. What to put in place before the invoices arrive Mitigation invoices begin arriving within weeks of landfall, and larger reconstruction bills follow for months. That gap is the time to prepare. Some insurers are already using automation to take on the time-intensive parts of invoice review, putting them in a better position to handle the next surge. A few decisions made now can keep review from becoming the bottleneck later: Confirm the rate agreements, pricing guidelines, and benchmarks reviewers will apply, including how post-storm pricing will be evaluated. Set one intake path for restoration invoices and define the supporting documentation each one needs. Identify which repeatable review steps, such as line-item extraction, arithmetic and rate checks, can be automated. Decide which findings can be resolved routinely and which require an adjuster or specialist. Decide in advance where overflow review goes if volume exceeds internal capacity. Claims teams cannot maintain catastrophe-level staffing through every quiet period. They need a review process that can expand when demand returns. Automating time-intensive invoice checks can help leaner teams absorb a surge without forcing a choice between longer cycle times and greater leakage. Restoration invoice auditing does not have to be a bottleneck, and keeping claims moving does not have to mean letting invoices pass through without scrutiny. Source notes Verisk ClaimSearch Trends Report, 2025 Year-end Analysis , p. 4. Commercial property claim counts are not directly comparable to the separate XactAnalysis assignment measure. Verisk Quarterly Property Report, April–June 2026 , pp. 3–4. Florida Office of Insurance Regulation, Hurricane Ian catastrophe claims data , as of March 4, 2025. Commercial property claims reported: 32,850; open with payment: 5,332; open without payment: 1,296; closed: 80%. Aggregate insurer-reported figures are unaudited and claim statuses can change. items.extracted_text: Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges | Insurance Thought Leadership Skip to main content Claims Automation Helps Claims Teams Handle Surges Hurricane Isaias shows how quickly claims surge after quiet periods, straining leaner teams to review complex restoration invoices thoroughly. Jeff Esper October 29, 2026 Hurricane Isaias spun up in the Gulf of Mexico and made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm on Oct. 9, just two days after becoming the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, the latest first hurricane in more than a century. Its sudden arrival is a reminder of how quickly a quiet claims environment can change. For property claims teams, the workload extends well beyond the initial wave of reported losses. Damage to hotels, apartment communities, retail centers and industrial properties can lead to large restoration projects and complex invoices that arrive over the weeks and months that follow. Early modeled estimates of privately insured losses range from $1 billion to $2 billion (Verisk) to $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion (Moody's RMS). While AM Best expects it to be an earnings event for insurers rather than a capital event, the storm created a substantial uptick in work for claims and restoration teams. The aerial imagery firm Vexcel counted about 17,860 damaged structures across Florida, Alabama and Mississippi, including more than 3,100 with major damage. A high-rise condominium resort on Pensacola Beach lost windows across two towers, and an apartment complex in Milton, Fla., lost much of its roof. Damage like that becomes restoration projects, and restoration projects become invoices. Isaias follows a prolonged stretch of slower claims activity. Industry data puts commercial property claims at 710,000 in 2025, down from 910,000 in 2023. A separate measure, U.S. property claim assignments , fell 12% year over year in the second quarter of 2026 and ran 13% below the five-year average, extending a four-year decline. These are different Verisk datasets, but both point to a slower claims environment. More of the work that remains also arrives in bursts: catastrophe claims made up 43% of second-quarter volume, up from 34% five years earlier. No claims organization can staff indefinitely for a catastrophe-level workload during a stretch like this. Nor should it. Teams that have adjusted staffing and resources to match lower demand face a particular challenge: claims volume can rebound much faster than review capacity can be rebuilt. When restoration invoices pile up, those leaner teams face a difficult trade-off. Bills can wait for a thorough audit, extending claim cycle times, or move through with less scrutiny, increasing the risk of leakage. Automation offers a way to absorb more work without having to rebuild the entire manual review operation. The surge also has a long tail. When Hurricane Sally struck the same stretch of coast in 2020, Florida insurers had closed about two-thirds of residential claims six weeks later, but only 13% of commercial property claims. Hurricane Ian made landfall in Florida on Sept. 28, 2022. In the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation's March 4, 2025, snapshot , 96% of the 789,066 reported Ian claims were closed. Yet 6,628 of the 32,850 commercial property claims remained open nearly two and a half years after the storm. Those figures do not establish whether the delays involved coverage, reconstruction, invoice review, or disputes. They do show how long commercial claims work can continue after the initial surge. The bottleneck moves as the claim progresses An initial wave of assignments is only the beginning. Adjusters must address coverage, communicate with insureds, inspect damage, review scopes and estimates, and coordinate recovery. Restoration invoices arrive as work progresses, often while those adjusters are still managing both new and existing claims. Large restoration projects can involve multiple crews, weeks of drying equipment, substantial material charges, and several subcontractors. The resulting invoices can be complex even under normal conditions. When many arrive together, claims teams face two pressures at once: more invoices to review and more work required to review each one thoroughly. An invoice is not simply a total to approve. Time-and-materials bills can require checking labor hours and classifications, equipment usage and duration, agreed rates, materials, subcontractor charges, markups, and arithmetic. A reviewer may need to compare the invoice with supporting records and the work performed. That takes time, and the work does not become less necessary because the team has fewer people available. Both delayed reviews and unsupported payments carry consequences for the insured, the carrier, and the restoration contractor waiting to be paid. Adding more reviewers can help, but it takes time to find, train, and coordinate them. It also raises the cost of handling a temporary spike. The more useful question is which repeatable parts of review can be completed consistently without requiring a few more hours of specialist time for every additional invoice. How automation can absorb a surge AI-enhanced automation can help teams review restoration invoices faster by extracting and sorting line items and running calculations to identify charges that need a closer look. During a surge, these capabilities support consistent, thorough review. AI can help turn invoice documents into organized data, while programmed audit rules check calculations and compare charges with agreed rates or benchmarks. The adjuster or specialist still has to consider the work performed, evaluate the findings, and resolve disagreements. Automation reduces the manual checking that precedes those decisions. Rest-Assured has pioneered the use of AI-enhanced automation in restoration invoice auditing. Property insurers have used the platform to audit nearly $1 billion in property restoration invoices, uncovering documented findings to guide claims professionals through review and resolution. Measure the effect on the claim The right measure is not merely how fast an audit comes back. Claims leaders should look at the time from invoice receipt to a documented review, how long exceptions take to resolve, the rate of confirmed findings, the cost per review, and whether payment disagreements are cleared sooner. Those measures show whether faster processing is actually helping the claim move toward resolution. What to put in place before the invoices arrive Mitigation invoices begin arriving within weeks of landfall, and larger reconstruction bills follow for months. That gap is the time to prepare. Some insurers are already using automation to take on the time-intensive parts of invoice review, putting them in a better position to handle the next surge. A few decisions made now can keep review from becoming the bottleneck later: Confirm the rate agreements, pricing guidelines, and benchmarks reviewers will apply, including how post-storm pricing will be evaluated. Set one intake path for restoration invoices and define the supporting documentation each one needs. Identify which repeatable review steps, such as line-item extraction, arithmetic and rate checks, can be automated. Decide which findings can be resolved routinely and which require an adjuster or specialist. Decide in advance where overflow review goes if volume exceeds internal capacity. Claims teams cannot maintain catastrophe-level staffing through every quiet period. They need a review process that can expand when demand returns. Automating time-intensive invoice checks can help leaner teams absorb a surge without forcing a choice between longer cycle times and greater leakage. Restoration invoice auditing does not have to be a bottleneck, and keeping claims moving does not have to mean letting invoices pass through without scrutiny. Commercial property claims reported: 32,850 open with payment: 5,332 open without payment: 1,296 closed: 80%. Aggregate insurer-reported figures are unaudited and claim statuses can change. Isaias timing: CBS News, citing NOAA records, Oct. 9, 2026 (first hurricane of the season on Oct. 7, the latest date in 121 years). Isaias insured loss estimates: Verisk, $1 billion to $2 billion onshore (Oct. 13, 2026) Moody's RMS, $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion private market (Oct. 16, 2026). AM Best and Vexcel figures as reported by Insurance Journal, Oct. 15, 2026. Florida Office of Insurance Regulation, Hurricane Sally claims data, as of Oct. 26, 2020. items.title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.original_title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.rss_title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.rss_description: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/26/2026 - 17:11 Bill Gross recently announced a free database of AI-generated ideas for innovative companies, based on the 31 methodologies that he's developed over the past three decades and that have powered his Idealab incubator. The list of ideas — currently totaling a whopping 1,208,580 — may or may not contain an idea that you'll be able to turn into big bucks, but I think that exploring the database and interacting with the ideas is worth a bit of your time. Many of the notions I see for the insurance market are provocative. They can at least suggest where there are holes in insurance offerings today that you should work to fill, even if you don't launch the sort of standalone company that Gross would love to see join his pioneering incubator. Let's have a look. Here is a link to the database . And here is a link to a Fortune article that describes the effort in detail, including Gross's argument that innovations driven by AI will create far more jobs than it will eliminate. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Once it had the customer base, it courted businesses — and the customer experience started to get gunked up by ads, attempts to keep customers from easily finding the best deals, etc. Once Amazon had built a marketplace where companies had to have a presence, it started milking them as much as possible on behalf of investors — a fee here, a fee there, maybe Amazon would even use its insights into sales data to launch products or businesses that would undercut a company with a hit offering on Amazon's platform. (Amazon has consistently denied doing so but has faced many lawsuits alleging it does.) Just about everybody still uses Amazon, but the experience is very different than it was a decade ago. Even if I'm right that there isn't a business in a "claims trust operating system," the Idealab database has still pointed to a sore spot that the insurance industry needs to address. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So insurers should at least be thinking about how they show their work, and quickly, to keep plaintiff attorneys from setting unrealistic expectations and accelerating the trend toward more and more litigation. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Once it had the customer base, it courted businesses — and the customer experience started to get gunked up by ads, attempts to keep customers from easily finding the best deals, etc. Once Amazon had built a marketplace where companies had to have a presence, it started milking them as much as possible on behalf of investors — a fee here, a fee there, maybe Amazon would even use its insights into sales data to launch products or businesses that would undercut a company with a hit offering on Amazon's platform. (Amazon has consistently denied doing so but has faced many lawsuits alleging it does.) Just about everybody still uses Amazon, but the experience is very different than it was a decade ago. Even if I'm right that there isn't a business in a "claims trust operating system," the Idealab database has still pointed to a sore spot that the insurance industry needs to address. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So insurers should at least be thinking about how they show their work, and quickly, to keep plaintiff attorneys from setting unrealistic expectations and accelerating the trend toward more and more litigation. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. items.extracted_text: SCOR sees competition from broker facilities, third-party capital as opportunity: CEO Léger - Artemis.bm SCOR sees competition from broker facilities, third-party capital as opportunity: CEO Léger - Artemis.bm SCOR sees competition from broker facilities, third-party capital as opportunity: CEO Léger 30th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Thierry Léger, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of global reinsurance firm SCOR, explained this morning that while the market is more competitive, with a proliferation of new capital entering, he sees this as an opportunity for the company, while suggesting that if there are better ways to match risk and capital they should be exploited. As our sister publication Reinsurance News reported earlier, SCOR delivered net income of €206 million in the third quarter of 2026 , driven by a strong group performance including a 3.5% rise in P&C insurance revenue to €1.9 billion and a combined ratio of 84.1%. SCOR’s results did highlight “deteriorating reinsurance margins” though, which is inevitable in a softened and highly competitive market environment. But the reinsurer’s CEO feels there are still attractive opportunities to be had, while the developments seen in the marketplace should not necessarily be viewed as negative. Commenting on the outlook for the end of year reinsurance renewals, Léger said, “Our P&C teams are now fully-focused on the 1st of January 2027 renewals. We expect competition to remain high and have a clear priority for our underwriters, margin and quality over volume. Over recent years, we have strengthened our capital discipline, remaining very selective and deploying capital only when risk-return is attractive. In the last weeks, we announced the exit of U.S. casualty and space of our direct insurance business due to lack of adequate margins and an unchanged negative outlook for these lines of business. Our tier one franchise technical expertise across P&C and life and health, and our strategic capital allocation to diversifying and profitable lines of business position us well ahead of the next strategic cycle and to navigate market headwinds.” Later during the call he was asked about how competition shows up in SCOR’s results, on which Léger acknowledged the inevitability that effects will be seen over-time. “Imagine it’s like a wave coming, and it’s coming also for us. So those results will slowly earn through IFRS 17, slowly earn through our quarterly results in the one to two years to come. We feel still limited impact from it, it’s still a bit too early, but we will see it next year, then the year after. “So there is pressure on the margins and we have been able to compensate the pressure with a bit more volume. So if you multiply volume times margins, we are still in a very good spot, and that’s really what we call portfolio steering. “We really try to steer our portfolio in the best possible way, allocate capacity, capital to the most attractive portfolios in a very dynamic way that allows us to still find attractive areas to grow. “But as I said at the beginning, we are in a more competitive environment. That’s what we are preparing for. I think that SCOR has very good cards to continue to write profitable business in the year to come.” During the call, Léger was asked for his views on broker-led reinsurance facilities in the market, which the CEO linked together with third-party capital and explained that it’s not necessarily all bad for the reinsurers. “On the broker-led reinsurance facilities, first of all we think that competition is there for a reason, right? I mean, if there are different ways, better ways to conduct business, then I think that’s what competition is here for. These things have to be exploited, these opportunitie,” Léger said. Continuing to explain that, “We see quite a dynamic and quite active broker environment, coming up with facilities that they haven’t maybe presented before. They’re using third-party capital in a way they haven’t done before, and so it’s not just the type of structures, they’re not new, but maybe the quantity of which come up right now probably a big link to the softening market. “However, for SCOR, we are always looking at those as an opportunity, what can we learn from it, what can we apply to us and how can we position SCOR in a nimble way to actually make those developments an opportunity. “So far, I would say it is much more in our camp now to react to it and understand what’s going on. I’m pretty confident that we will be able to make it an opportunity for SCOR, accepting that the environment is what it is, and we have to adapt and we have to make the best out of it.” SCOR is already utilising third-party capital within its business in numerous ways, from its retrocession purchases, to risk-sharing arrangements and of course its asset management arm SCOR Investment Partners through its insurance-linked securities (ILS) funds. During the Monte Carlo reinsurance event, Léger had said that the reinsurer sees third-party capital as an attractive source of capital for the firm, and sees no future changes regarding its strategy for managing it . Naturally, the largest reinsurance companies in the world have sufficient access to underwriting flow, as well as the data to support major investors entry into the market in support of their business, which positions players like SCOR to lean more heavily on third-party investors should they choose to. At a time when brokers are pulling significant new capital into a softening market, the reinsurers natural and best response may be to identify how these trends can be leant into, to help them make their own businesses more efficient as well. items.title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.original_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_title: Buy or Build? Yes.
items.rss_description: Buy or Build? Yes. Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:49 AI has lowered barriers to building custom insurance workflows, but integration and adoption remain the hardest parts of implementation. October 26, 2026 Image One of my takeaways from ITC Vegas this fall was that a lot of vendors are playing defense. A lot of carriers are looking at what AI can do now and asking some version of the same question: Hold on a minute, the world changed, so should we just build everything ourselves? It's a fair question. The barriers to building have come down a lot in the last year, and the benefits of owning your own technology are real. When a convincing demo takes a couple of engineers instead of a sales cycle, the old reasons to buy start to look pretty thin. I suppose I'm not the most neutral person to ask. I've spent the last decade building and running Clearcover , an AI-native carrier, and now Dearborn Labs , an AI-native software development firm built specifically for insurance; if anyone was going to tell you to build everything, it would probably be me. But when people ask me whether to buy or build, my answer is...yes. We have components of our system that we bought and didn't build, and we're fine with that. We build more than we buy, though, and more every day. Is "yes" a dodge? Maybe a little. Mostly it's that buy vs. build was never one decision. Every carrier already runs a mix of both, workflow by workflow. And even the build half of my answer comes with an asterisk. Where should the line sit? The choices sit along a spectrum, made one workflow at a time, and lately the mix has been shifting toward build. That makes sense to me, and I'd expect it to keep shifting for as long as building keeps getting cheaper. Buy what's already solved well. If a problem looks roughly the same at every carrier, and someone has spent years getting good at it, there isn't much to gain from building your own version, and the time and money are better spent elsewhere. But that list gets shorter every month. Build the workflows where being different is the point, like how you triage a new claim or decide which risks to write. Buying those means working the same way as everyone else who bought the same thing, which probably isn't what you were going for. Where exactly that line falls depends a lot on the carrier and its lines of business, which is why a single company-wide decision on buy vs. build usually ends up wrong somewhere. The asterisk What qualifies as building, because you can put a demo together, is usually the smallest portion of the work. AI can change how a claim moves and which decisions get made without a person ever opening the file, but the systems underneath that workflow rarely change, or at least they rarely change quickly. Not everybody is doing a rip-and-replace of their whole company to launch a new AI workflow. A new claims-intake workflow still has to post to your core system and set reserves the way your actuaries expect, and an underwriting workbench still has to read from policy admin and write its decisions back. None of that shows up in a demo. The interface is mostly a solved problem now, and that's good news. The hard part is the wiring underneath it. Most of the AI conversations I have with carriers wind up being about traditional software engineering. That's the work of fitting whatever the AI application or agent is into the rest of the company, so the systems supporting a reinvented workflow still work properly. And the wiring is only half of the asterisk. The other half is running the thing in production until people actually work that way. Most implementation projects are scoped to end at go-live, which is roughly where this half starts. At Clearcover, adoption of the AI tools across our claims team is 92%+. A number like that gets earned after go-live, inside real claims, over however long it takes for the new way of working to become just how the job gets done. You might reasonably ask whether all of this is an argument for buying something that comes already integrated. For the work that's solved well, it is. But a bought workflow is the vendor's workflow, designed to fit as many carriers as possible, and in the workflows you'd want to run differently from everyone else, that's exactly the problem. Build realistically. Before you build a new workflow, ask three questions of it: Foundation — Was this workflow designed around constraints that no longer exist? Fit — Can it work with the systems you already have, without a rip and replace? Engineering — Do your engineers own the integration layer today, and can you test, govern and audit what runs on it? The first is about not building on top of a bad foundation. A lot of insurance workflows were shaped by limits that made sense at the time, like a handoff that existed because two systems couldn't talk to each other, or a sampling audit that existed because nobody could read every file. If you automate that workflow as it stands, what you get is the old process running a little faster, and you've spent real money to keep a constraint you no longer have. The second one is more encouraging. You don't have to fully rip out your systems to improve a workflow, so long as you have the software engineering chops to fit the new workflow into the systems you have. The third is the one I'd push on hardest, mostly because a demo is very good at hiding it. If the answer is no, I'd want to know that before the demo goes in front of the Board rather than after. If you're asking me whether to buy or build, I'd say build more than you used to. Just go in knowing that the demo is the easy part, and that the wiring, plus the long stretch of running it until people actually work that way, is the job. So where does your line sit this year, and who's doing the wiring? Kyle Nakatsuji

items.summary: Buy or Build? Yes. Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:49 AI has lowered barriers to building custom insurance workflows, but integration and adoption remain the hardest parts of implementation. October 26, 2026 Image One of my takeaways from ITC Vegas this fall was that a lot of vendors are playing defense. A lot of carriers are looking at what AI can do now and asking some version of the same question: Hold on a minute, the world changed, so should we just build everything ourselves? It's a fair question. The barriers to building have come down a lot in the last year, and the benefits of owning your own technology are real. When a convincing demo takes a couple of engineers instead of a sales cycle, the old reasons to buy start to look pretty thin. I suppose I'm not the most neutral person to ask. I've spent the last decade building and running Clearcover , an AI-native carrier, and now Dearborn Labs , an AI-native software development firm built specifically for insurance; if anyone was going to tell you to build everything, it would probably be me. But when people ask me whether to buy or build, my answer is...yes. We have components of our system that we bought and didn't build, and we're fine with that. We build more than we buy, though, and more every day. Is "yes" a dodge? Maybe a little. Mostly it's that buy vs. build was never one decision. Every carrier already runs a mix of both, workflow by workflow. And even the build half of my answer comes with an asterisk. Where should the line sit? The choices sit along a spectrum, made one workflow at a time, and lately the mix has been shifting toward build. That makes sense to me, and I'd expect it to keep shifting for as long as building keeps getting cheaper. Buy what's already solved well. If a problem looks roughly the same at every carrier, and someone has spent years getting good at it, there isn't much to gain from building your own version, and the time and money are better spent elsewhere. But that list gets shorter every month. Build the workflows where being different is the point, like how you triage a new claim or decide which risks to write. Buying those means working the same way as everyone else who bought the same thing, which probably isn't what you were going for. Where exactly that line falls depends a lot on the carrier and its lines of business, which is why a single company-wide decision on buy vs. build usually ends up wrong somewhere. The asterisk What qualifies as building, because you can put a demo together, is usually the smallest portion of the work. AI can change how a claim moves and which decisions get made without a person ever opening the file, but the systems underneath that workflow rarely change, or at least they rarely change quickly. Not everybody is doing a rip-and-replace of their whole company to launch a new AI workflow. A new claims-intake workflow still has to post to your core system and set reserves the way your actuaries expect, and an underwriting workbench still has to read from policy admin and write its decisions back. None of that shows up in a demo. The interface is mostly a solved problem now, and that's good news. The hard part is the wiring underneath it. Most of the AI conversations I have with carriers wind up being about traditional software engineering. That's the work of fitting whatever the AI application or agent is into the rest of the company, so the systems supporting a reinvented workflow still work properly. And the wiring is only half of the asterisk. The other half is running the thing in production until people actually work that way. Most implementation projects are scoped to end at go-live, which is roughly where this half starts. At Clearcover, adoption of the AI tools across our claims team is 92%+. A number like that gets earned after go-live, inside real claims, over however long it takes for the new way of working to become just how the job gets done. You might reasonably ask whether all of this is an argument for buying something that comes already integrated. For the work that's solved well, it is. But a bought workflow is the vendor's workflow, designed to fit as many carriers as possible, and in the workflows you'd want to run differently from everyone else, that's exactly the problem. Build realistically. Before you build a new workflow, ask three questions of it: Foundation — Was this workflow designed around constraints that no longer exist? Fit — Can it work with the systems you already have, without a rip and replace? Engineering — Do your engineers own the integration layer today, and can you test, govern and audit what runs on it? The first is about not building on top of a bad foundation. A lot of insurance workflows were shaped by limits that made sense at the time, like a handoff that existed because two systems couldn't talk to each other, or a sampling audit that existed because nobody could read every file. If you automate that workflow as it stands, what you get is the old process running a little faster, and you've spent real money to keep a constraint you no longer have. The second one is more encouraging. You don't have to fully rip out your systems to improve a workflow, so long as you have the software engineering chops to fit the new workflow into the systems you have. The third is the one I'd push on hardest, mostly because a demo is very good at hiding it. If the answer is no, I'd want to know that before the demo goes in front of the Board rather than after. If you're asking me whether to buy or build, I'd say build more than you used to. Just go in knowing that the demo is the easy part, and that the wiring, plus the long stretch of running it until people actually work that way, is the job. So where does your line sit this year, and who's doing the wiring? Kyle Nakatsuji

items.extracted_text: The Hartford returns with $280m target for Foundation Re IV 2027-1 cat bond - Artemis.bm The Hartford returns with $280m target for Foundation Re IV 2027-1 cat bond - Artemis.bm The Hartford returns with $280m target for Foundation Re IV 2027-1 cat bond 30th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans The Hartford, a US primary property and casualty insurer, has returned to the catastrophe bond market with an initial target to secure $280 million or more in multi-peril collateralized catastrophe reinsurance protection from the capital markets through sponsorship of a Foundation Re IV Ltd. (Series 2027-1) cat bond issuance, Artemis has learned. This latest catastrophe bond from The Hartford will become the eighth transaction is has sponsored since it brought to market the first in the Foundation Re cat bond series of deals back in 2004. A year ago, The Hartford secured $270 million of multi-peril reinsurance from the capital markets through the Foundation Re IV Ltd. (Series 2026-1) catastrophe bond. That issuance, coming within two years of the one prior, showed The Hartford looking to begin layering cat bonds within its reinsurance tower and staggering the maturities of the capital markets coverage. Now, returning just one year later, it seems that strategy is set to continue. As we reported earlier this year, The Hartford has also been using its cat bonds to meaningfully raise the top of its occurrence catastrophe reinsurance tower . Before turning to the new cat bond, the Hartford has $200 million of multi-peril catastrophe reinsurance from the Foundation Re IV 2023-1 issuance that matures around the end of 2026, so it’s good to see this new offering starting at a larger size. You can read about every Foundation Re catastrophe bond from The Hartford in our extensive Deal Directory . The Hartford is set to use Bermuda-based special purpose insurer (SPI) Foundation Re IV Ltd. for the third time as the issuing vehicle for its latest catastrophe bond. Foundation Re IV Ltd. is offering investors a single tranche of Series 2027-1 Class A notes, with the proceeds from their sale set to be used to collateralize a reinsurance agreement between the issuer and ceding company, with the beneficiaries being Hartford Fire Insurance Co. and subsidiaries, sources explained. The initial target is to secure at least $280 million of protection with this Series 2027-1 issuance, with the targeted reinsurance being fully-collateralized US named storm and earthquake protection, including for D.C. and Puerto Rico, across a four calendar year term running to the end of 2030. This latest Foundation Re IV cat bond from The Hartford will feature an indemnity trigger and provide coverage on a per-occurrence basis, just like its last. The initial attachment point for the coverage will be at $1.3 billion of losses, covering a share up to $1.7 billion, giving room for this new cat bond from the Hartford to upsize to fill this $400 million layer should the sponsor choose. The currently $280 million of Foundation Re IV Ltd. Series 2027-1 Class A notes that are being offered will come with an initial attachment probability of 1.93%, an initial base expected loss of 1.56% and they are being offered to cat bond investors with spread price guidance in a range from 3% to 3.5%, we understand. We can compare the risk-level and price guidance with how The Hartford’s last two cat bond settled. The soon to mature Foundation Re IV 2023 cat bond had an initial attachment point of $1.1 billion, an expected loss was 1.36% and the notes initially paid investors a spread of 6.25%, so a significantly higher multiple-at-market than these new notes are being offered at. Last year’s Foundation Re IV 2026-1 cat bond attached initially at $1.6 billion of losses, with an expected loss of 1.18% and priced to pay investors a spread of 3.5%, so again a higher multiple than this new 2027-1 offering. Given the strong price execution being seen in the catastrophe bond market at this time, it will be interesting to see whether The Hartford looks to increase the size of its latest offering, given the cost-effective reinsurance cat bonds are providing to sponsors at this time. You can read all about this new Foundation Re IV Ltd. (Series 2027-1) cat bond transaction in our Deal Directory , where you can analyse details of almost every catastrophe bond ever issued. items.extracted_text: Wrongful Data Collection Driving Cyber Claim Frequency Article 0 Comments A growing source of cyber insurance claims is wrongful data collection. Even though the cost of these claims individually is generally low, their rising frequency should be of concern to underwriters and policyholders. California has now narrowed one of the legal theories behind these claims, but the exposure is far from over. Wrongful data collection claims typically result in settlements between $10,000 and $30,000, far below the multimillion-dollar losses common in ransomware claims. In its Midyear Cyber Risk Report, Resilience found ransomware and extortion claims accounted for nearly 75% of cyber claim costs in the first half of 2026, making them high on the severity scale. Wrongful data collection lawsuits, on the other hand, were the third-largest source of cyber losses, at less than 4%, behind transfer fraud, which accounted for about 9%. Jeremy Gittler Ransomware and wrongful data collection claims also differ in their frequency. Lawsuits alleging wrongful data collection appeared in 16.7% of all Resilience cyber claims in the first half of 2026, up from 7.3% a year earlier. Why the Claims Have Been Growing What is causing the increase? Wrongful data collection lawsuits are becoming more frequent due to two overarching trends: Proliferation of website visitor tracking and data sharing with third parties. Virtually every website collects information on visitors, and consumer businesses want to know their customers’ buying habits. This isn’t necessarily nefarious, but the widespread collection of data creates opportunity for plaintiffs. State and federal laws governing data privacy. Plaintiffs are filing lawsuits under the California Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA), the federal Wiretap Act, and the California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act. Many recent cases rely on two parts of CIPA: Section 638.51, which targets “pen register” and “trap and trace” devices, and Section 631, which addresses wiretapping. The legal theory is essentially the same in all wrongful data collection claims: company websites are tracking people and sharing that data without their consent, in violation of one or more laws. In practice, plaintiffs are following two different approaches. One is from pro se plaintiffs, who represent themselves, typically under CIPA. These are high-volume, low-severity cases that may be resolved within a client’s self-insured retention. A second type of wrongful data collection claim is more intricate, brought by law firms. These range from demand letters to outright lawsuits, often under California laws, the federal Wiretap Act and other laws. Large corporations and organizations with experienced in-house counsel typically are aware of data collection requirements and how to mitigate complaints. Smaller businesses are preferred targets for high-volume claims. Serial filers know it’s inexpensive to send demand letters or complaints and seek quick settlements. Most plaintiffs do not have an appetite or budget for protracted litigation, and many defendants view these claims as a cost of doing business. California’s response is likely to change that calculus. On Sept. 30, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed SB 690, which ends the private right of action for claims under CIPA’s pen register and trap-and-trace provision (Section 638.51) when the conduct occurs on a website, online application or mobile application. Plaintiffs had argued that cookies, pixels and analytics tools fall under that section, and its $5,000 per-violation statutory damages made demand letters and complaints attractive to serial filers. For that conduct, only the California attorney general may now bring those claims. The law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027, and applies to pending claims in actions commenced on or after Jan. 1, 2025. Pre-suit demand letters that never became lawsuits may fall outside that reach, and plaintiffs are expected to challenge retroactive application. SB 690 does not end the exposure. It leaves private claims under CIPA’s wiretapping provisions and the federal Wiretap Act untouched, and plaintiffs have already begun shifting to those theories. Frequency of Section 638.51 claims, particularly the high-volume pro se filings, may fall, but claims under the remaining laws could continue and may be more costly to defend. The high frequency of wrongful data collection claims could create large aggregate losses for cyber insurers, if retentions remain low or the costs of defending, including discovery, increase. At the moment, the aggregate loss line for such claims is flat. Whether SB 690 reduces frequency or simply redirects claims will become clearer in 2027. Coverage Questions Coverage of wrongful data collection claims in cyber insurance is not uniform. Under some policies, the claims trigger coverage, while others don’t. Some policies exclude wrongful data collection. The industry does not have a singular approach to these kinds of claims. SB 690 may prompt some insurers to revisit their wording, and retroactivity could affect how pending claims are reserved. Cyber underwriters should inquire about data collection practices to ensure a policyholder is not violating the law. Questions to ask include: What data are you collecting? Which tracking tools (pixels, analytics, session replay, chat) are on your website, and are they configured to honor visitor consent? How long are you holding that data? Do you inform your customers that you’re collecting their data? Is the data collection obvious? Is your organization sharing that data with anyone else? Collecting data on website visitors is not by itself the problem. The laws’ intent is to protect privacy by requiring notification and consent of those whose data is collected and shared. Insurance exists to offer protection when a policyholder does everything right, but a loss still happens. The cyber insurance industry will have to sort out the question of whether data collection is an insurable business activity or should be excluded. Mitigation Tips Organizations can mitigate the risk of wrongful data collection lawsuits by taking several actions. These include: Improve risk governance. Organizations should ensure compliance with all applicable laws. This generally includes informing site visitors if tracking tools are collecting and sharing their data, and recording users’ consent. SB 690 is not a reason to scale back consent practices, because the wiretapping theories that remain turn on notice and consent. Communicate data collection internally. Tracking site visitors and monitoring their online behaviors is typically done for valid business reasons, such as to improve the marketing of products or services. The marketing team, however, might fail to discuss the use of data collection tools with the general counsel or chief financial officer. Internal departments need to talk to each other, so all teams remain aware of legal requirements. Manage third-party risks. Organizations that use vendors to gather data on their behalf will be responsible at the outset even if a vendor wrongfully collected the data. Contractual risk transfer, with indemnity and hold-harmless agreements, can mitigate third-party risks. Recourse also can occur through subrogation. Liability exposure arising from wrongful data collection can be reduced with appropriate protocols and well-constructed cyber risk management programs. Organizations should work with their legal and risk advisors and cyber insurance partners to maximize the benefits of data collection while minimizing the risks.
